questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the name "Saheb-e-Alam," and what is the ironic contrast between this meaning and Saheb's actual life in the chapter?
questions.a: The literal meaning is "lord of the universe." The irony is that Saheb is a barefoot ragpicker who scrounges in garbage dumps, owns nothing, and has no control over his life — the exact opposite of a lord. A wrong answer (e.g., "his name means he is rich") reveals the student misses that irony requires a contradiction between label and reality, not just a mismatch.

questions.q: In the text, the author says: "Garbage to them is gold." Explain why this statement is an example of irony, not just a metaphor.
questions.a: It is situational irony because garbage — waste, filth, something discarded — becomes "gold" (value, hope, survival) only due to the extreme poverty that forces children to scavenge. The irony lies in the perverse inversion: what is worthless to society becomes precious to the poor. A student who calls it only a metaphor misses the bitter contradiction that the "gold" is still garbage, and the children's hope is built on society's refuse.

questions.q: Saheb takes a job at a tea stall for 800 rupees and meals. The author notes: "The steel canister seems heavier than the plastic bag he would carry so lightly over his shoulder. The bag was his. The canister belongs to the man who owns the tea shop. Saheb is no longer his own master!" Identify the symbol in this passage and explain what it represents.
questions.a: The steel canister symbolizes the loss of autonomy and the burden of child labor. Unlike the plastic bag (symbol of freedom, self-directed work), the canister is owned by the employer, making Saheb a servant. A wrong answer (e.g., "the canister represents his income") focuses on the literal function and misses the symbolic weight: the object embodies the theft of childhood and agency.

questions.q: Compare the symbolism of bangles in the two worlds described in Firozabad: (a) the bangles as "symbol of an Indian woman's suhaag, auspiciousness in marriage" and (b) the bangles made by children in "dark hutments" who "lose their eyesight before they become adults." What does this dual symbolism reveal about the chapter's central theme?
questions.a: The bangle is a symbol of cultural sanctity and marital auspiciousness for the wearer, but a symbol of exploitation, blindness, and stolen childhood for the maker. This duality reveals the chapter's core theme: the beauty of tradition is built on the invisible suffering of the poor. A weak answer describes only one side (e.g., "bangles are auspicious") and fails to analyze the contradiction that the same object carries opposite meanings for different classes.

questions.q: The author writes: "Few airplanes fly over Firozabad." Evaluate whether this statement functions primarily as literal description, symbolism, or irony — and justify your evaluation with textual evidence.
questions.a: It functions as symbolism (and subtle irony). Literally, it notes low air traffic; symbolically, it represents the limited horizons of children like Mukesh, who dreams of cars but not planes because planes are unimaginable in his world. The irony: airplanes symbolize freedom and global connection, but Firozabad — a town that makes bangles for the world — is cut off from that world. A student who calls it only "literal description" misses the author's deliberate use of a passing detail to encapsulate systemic entrapment.

questions.q: Create a new symbolic object for a hypothetical third story in "Lost Spring" about a child working in a fireworks factory in Sivakasi. Name the object, describe its literal form, and explain what it would symbolize about the child's life, mirroring the depth of the bangles or the steel canister.
questions.a: Example: A "singed kite string" (manjha) — literally, the coated string used to fly kites, made by the child. It symbolizes the razor-thin line between celebration and danger: the same string that brings joy in the sky cuts the hands that make it. A poor answer invents an object without linking its literal properties to the child's dual reality (e.g., "a firecracker — it symbolizes danger" is too obvious and lacks the layered irony of the original symbols).
